Likelihood objects for the benchmark

Source: R/04_00_likelihoods.R
population_likelihood.Rd

population_likelihood() is the Gaussian convolution \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}, \sum_j p_j^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)\); single_cell_likelihood() is the mixture of cells, with its two scales \((c,\phi)\) profiled out, so every function is evaluated at the closed-form scales of the composition. They play the part of stats::family() in stats::glm(): deconvolute_ratios() and run_simulation_benchmark() take one as likelihood, either the object or the constructor itself.

Usage

population_likelihood()

single_cell_likelihood()

Value

An object of class decovart_likelihood.

Details

Each object is a list of class decovart_likelihood with

  • name: "population" or "single_cell";

  • nuisance: whether the model has the scales \((c,\phi)\);

  • parameters(cell_names): the rows of every interval matrix, the cell types and, for the single-cell model, mean_scale, variance_scale, platform_scale_a and cell_count_n;

  • simulate(mean, Sigma, theta, n): n bulk samples drawn from the moments mean and Sigma with the composition and settings in theta; returns Y, the target truth and the true scales nuisance (NULL for the population model);

  • loglik(p, y, mu, Sigma), score(p, y, mu, Sigma), se(p, y, mu, Sigma) (Wald standard errors of the composition) and curvature(p, y, mu, Sigma) (local-maximum flag and eigenvalue range of the Hessian in ILR coordinates, NA on the boundary);

  • interval(method, y, p_hat, p_true, mu, Sigma, ci): one method of the interval menu at the estimate p_hat, as a two-column matrix.

The interval methods are

  • wald: delta method on \(\boldsymbol{p}\), symmetric;

  • ilr: Wald interval in ILR coordinates mapped back to the simplex;

  • profile: likelihood-ratio inversion; it refits from y, so it does not depend on the solver that produced p_hat;

  • bootstrap: percentile interval of a parametric bootstrap refitted by ci$optimiser;

  • oracle: p_hat plus or minus the Wald half-width evaluated at the true composition.

For the single-cell model, _reml appended to wald, ilr or profile applies the REML calibration (\(\nu=G-J\)), and Wald, ILR and bootstrap intervals also cover the scales and the derived \(a=\phi/c\) and \(n=c^{2}/\phi\).

Wald, ILR and oracle intervals are undefined when p_hat has a zero coordinate: on a face (one zero), an edge (two zeros) or a vertex (\(J-1\) zeros, one cell type making up the whole sample). L-BFGS-B returns such estimates; Newton-Raphson in ILR coordinates does not. Their rows are then NA, scales included, and the coverage of these methods is conditional on an interior estimate.

See also

deconvolute_ratios(), run_simulation_benchmark()

Examples

mu <- matrix(c(20, 22, 22, 20), 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("a", "b")))
Sigma <- array(c(diag(2), diag(2)), dim = c(2, 2, 2))
lik <- population_likelihood()
lik
#> <decovart_likelihood: population>
y <- drop(mu %*% c(0.4, 0.6))
lik$loglik(c(0.4, 0.6), y, mu, Sigma)
#> [1] 0.6539265
kkt_residual(c(0.4, 0.6), lik$score(c(0.4, 0.6), y, mu, Sigma))
#> [1] 0.5439283
single_cell_likelihood()$parameters(c("a", "b"))
#> [1] "a"                "b"                "mean_scale"       "variance_scale"  
#> [5] "platform_scale_a" "cell_count_n"
